The principal method is a five-year, monthly, post-rent owner-earnings P/E model. Cash interest and principal repayment are explicit, all new debt and rescue equity alter debt/shares, and the terminal price is earnings value divided by terminal diluted shares. Accumulated CFO is not also added as surplus cash; dividends are zero. Debt is not subtracted a second time from an equity earnings multiple. A separate operating FCFF DCF uses 12/15/18% WACC and 2/4/6% terminal growth with explicit reinvestment g/15% assumed terminal ROIC, netting entry debt and only excess cash. Its entry claims are hypothetical and it is a diagnostic cross-check, not a second investable target. [MODEL]

The bear/base/bull operating cases link store cohorts and non-retail demand to gross margin, cash rent and operating expense, then to tax, capex, deposits, inventory, receivables, supplier advances, payables and principal. Cash interest is computed on opening debt; new debt raised within a period begins interest next month, a simplifying assumption that postpones rather than conservatively increases expense. D&A is a percentage of opening PPE, not a presumed maintenance requirement. Maintenance capex is 1% of annualized sales plus new-store fit-outs; maintenance needs are ND, so this is sensitized rather than certified owner earnings. Annual model years are rolling periods from entry, not falsely labeled statutory FY27–FY31.

March-to-entry cash is reconstructed with analyst assumptions and the provisional H1 revenue total, plus exact October receipts. Monthly pre-entry borrowing or rescue requirements are counterfactual requirements, not evidence that such share issues occurred; actual issued shares remain separately 10,391,550. The unknown interim cash/balance prevents a supported entry state. Within forecast months, a front-loaded payment stress deducts capex, deposits, working-capital investment, debt service and 25% of cash operating costs before collections. This assumption tests timing, not an observed bank calendar. [S07, S09, S10; MODEL]

Four funding policies are separate: no new funding, hypothetical ₹20 crore new debt, that debt plus a hard ₹30 crore gross equity-rescue cap, and an explicitly unlimited-equity mathematical counterfactual. Rescue issuance is at ₹264.60, 40% below the observed price, with 3% fees and shares rounded up to whole shares, subject to a hard gross-cap check. No lender/investor commitment is implied. Future warrant cash enters only in the two equity policies; actual upfront receipts are never repeated. Breached paths may continue solely to display unfunded counterfactual arithmetic. Their ordinary terminal price and IRR are null. Even paths funded within their assumed cap have ordinary returns suppressed because current entry liquidity and assumed pre-entry financing are unverified. [MODEL]

Two-way operating-growth/multiple and collection/inventory sensitivities rerun financing and dilution. Reverse expectations solve the same linked model for 12%, 15% and 18% return hurdles at fixed terminal multiples, retaining bracket and residual checks; an unlimited funding solution proves only mathematical scale, not financing feasibility. Entry ceilings are non-actionable conditional arithmetic. R, D and P remain NS. A price cannot be declared attractive by selecting an optimistic, unfunded terminal outcome.

The 60 observed official sessions have mean traded value ₹12.3175 million and median ₹10.6709 million; the 20-session mean is ₹13.6135 million and median ₹11.0043 million. There are no missing or observed zero-volume sessions in the 60-date sample and one one-price session. At 5% of the lower 60-day mean/median, a ₹5 lakh notional exit takes 0.9371 theoretical days. The minimum lot is 250 shares, costing ₹110,250: four lots cost ₹441,000 and five ₹551,250. The rounded-up five-lot position takes 1.0332 theoretical days, but only four whole lots fit the conservative 5% daily share-volume allowance, implying at least two sessions. Results at 2%/10% participation are retained. Historical ST observations are included before the later SM series; absent symbols are never silently treated as zero. Exact live spreads, order-book depth and executable limit-circuit exits are ND. [S23]

"DUR is 6: repeated child-replacement demand, underpenetrated localities and multiple distribution channels offer a credible accessible runway, but a national market-size headline does not establish profitable site-level demand. The operating path is bottom-up: productive mature stores plus cohort maturation plus new stores, combined with separately modeled non-retail sales. Every store requires fit-out capital, opening stock, lease deposits, recurring rent, staff and promotional spending. Wholesale growth requires collectible receivables and supplier funding. Store count cannot grow without those balance-sheet commitments. [S01, S07, S12–S13]

The model tests 10/30/50 annual gross store additions, mature company-store annual sales of ₹0.90/₹1.20/₹1.44 crore, and 0%/6%/10% mature-store growth. Ninety percent company ownership is an analyst assumption, not a verified September mix. New cohorts ramp over twelve months; existing stores also mature. Rent, staffing/other costs, inventory, vendor advances, receivables, capex and security deposits all move with scale. These scenarios are deliberately conditional because store-by-store actual invested capital and audited profitability are absent. No management EBITDA percentage is treated as project IRR. [MODEL assumptions]

Management said store EBITDA was approximately 16% for all 109 outlets, 20% excluding the last six months' openings and 22% for stores older than a year. It also described 4–6 month breakeven. Those statements could indicate maturing economics, but the inclusion of central costs, rent normalization, depreciation, stock markdowns, inventory and deposits is not fully defined. Cash payback and project ROIC therefore remain NS. A whole-company one-year incremental ROIC proxy is calculated at 10.77%, below the illustrative 12–18% nominal operating-capital-cost range. Timing and unresolved balances make that diagnostic, not proof of project value destruction or the CAP score. Three- and five-year comparable capital bridges are unavailable. [S07, S12]

Growth is demonstrably cash demanding. Financing-stripped CFO was negative in FY24, FY25 and FY26 even before capex. The new October raise provides capital but creates more claims on future earnings. GQS remains NS with a persistent-cash cap at 5 if missing factors become scoreable. A healthy runway requires improving collections and stock turns while new cohorts mature, not indefinite dilution at optimistic prices.

The prospectus provides individual-store sales for twenty named locations through H1FY25. These observations are retained in a dedicated table rather than replaced by an invented mature-cohort dataset. Opening dates are disclosed on prospectus page 75. Five stores opened before FY22; Ghaziabad opened in December 2021 and Bhucho Mandi in February 2022. The seven-store group totals ₹2.8003 crore in FY22 and ₹7.2122 crore in FY24, so its growth includes two partial-year ramps. The five pre-FY22 stores are separately calculated as a dated common-store sales diagnostic, not current normalized same-store growth or project returns. Patiala later closed/relocated. A further conflict is explicit: page 75 dates the Patiala–Bhupendra Nagar replacement opening to 9 November 2024, while page 129 attributes ₹17.94 lakh sales to H1 ended 30 September 2024. That row is not used as clean cohort evidence. The full historical channel totals also exceed statutory operations revenue by small amounts, so no exact channel-to-statutory reconciliation is claimed. The regional risk table contains percentages that do not consistently match its displayed NCR amounts and denominators; geographic percentage claims therefore remain qualified. "MOAT is 4: a differentiated brand proposition and expanding distribution exist, but durable pricing power, high retention and superior mature-store returns are not demonstrated. Children's replacement demand supports a category runway; it does not guarantee that this brand captures it. Consumers can switch among specialist labels, marketplaces, department stores, value retailers and unorganized sellers. Fashion risk, discounting, sourcing concentration and changing fit/style preferences limit permanence. Store count and a high reported gross margin alone are not moat evidence. The company's prospectus explicitly describes intense competition and competitors with more financial resources and greater brand recognition. [S01 risks; S12–S13]

Three economic comparators frame the test, without forcing inappropriate peer multiples. Brainbees/FirstCry combines mother-and-child products, third-party and home brands, online activity, owned stores, franchise distribution and international operations; its platform scope is not Purple's single-brand wholesale/retail perimeter. Cantabil is a broader family-apparel store operator and a useful benchmark for mature-store sales, lease-adjusted returns and rollout discipline, but not a matched kidswear multiple. S.P. Apparels' garment-manufacturing model is a deliberately contrasting supplier-side comparator: production scale and export/customer qualification cannot be borrowed as Purple's moat. No comparable-date peer valuation ranking or claim of superior peer financial quality is made without harmonized primary accounts. [S25–S27]

The highest-value test is evidence that repeat demand survives lower promotions and that older stores earn adequate cash returns after inventory and deposits. Management's 26% repeat-customer measure lacks a disclosed customer cohort and observation window. Fourteen older stores' claimed 26% growth is encouraging, but not independently reconciled to full-year like-for-like revenue. A stronger brand would show durable realized prices, lower markdown losses, stable retention and growing mature-cohort cash returns despite competition. [S12–S13]"

"Purple United Sales is an outsourced children's-apparel brand, merchandise distributor and rapidly expanding store operator, not a manufacturing-capacity moat. Revenue and store openings have accelerated, but the decisive question is whether mature stores and wholesale collections earn cash returns on the full inventory, deposits and fit-out capital. FY26 revenue rose 65.46% to ₹170.6321 crore while reported operating cash flow was negative ₹9.2858 crore. Removing identifiable financing classifications makes CFO negative ₹13.1999 crore; cash after capex and interest was negative ₹45.6843 crore. Recurring confirmation discrepancies, weak comparable growth and cohort evidence, and unknown October cash/headroom prevent a supported five-year equity-return forecast. "The Purple United Kids brand sells apparel, footwear and accessories for children through exclusive brand outlets, distributors/general trade, key accounts and online channels. Products are sourced as traded merchandise from external manufacturers. Its operational advantages, if proven, would be design, assortment, sourcing, consumer recognition and route-to-market, not ownership of low-cost factories. Reported purchases and changes in merchandise inventory therefore matter more than plant utilization. Store fit-outs, rent deposits, merchandise and wholesale credit absorb capital even when manufacturing is outsourced. [S01 business pp.123–134; S07 notes 16–23]

The September presentation reports FY25 channel mix of 21% retail, 3% online, 5% key accounts and 71% distribution; FY26 mix becomes 40%, 2%, 20% and 38%. These are management percentages, not audited segment financials. Applying them mechanically gives a directional channel bridge, but approximate shares and shifting classification prevent a precise organic-growth attribution. Lower distributor share does not mean lower absolute distributor sales or automatically better cash collection. Key accounts can carry credit, and retail stores require inventory before sale. Inter-branch transfers are eliminated from statutory revenue: FY26 gross revenue of ₹245.2966 crore less ₹74.6645 crore transfers equals ₹170.6321 crore net sales. Counting transfers as customer demand would materially overstate scale. [S07 note 16; S13]

The network grew from 14 outlets in March 2024 to 43 in March 2025, 109 in March 2026 and 126 in September 2026. The prospectus' FY23 channel table says 11 while another narrative says 12; the discrepancy is retained. Total stores are not equivalent to company-owned stores, mature stores, average stores open during a year or comparable-store sales. Management described roughly 8–10 franchise stores in May; the exact September ownership mix and closure history remain ND. [S01, S11–S13]

The prospectus describes an India-only business and 45–90 day customer/distributor credit terms, with no assurance of long-term commitments. Current top-customer and top-supplier percentages were not located; the prospectus statement that revenue is not dependent on a few customers is a company assertion, not a quantified concentration test. Key-account logos and marketplace availability establish routes to market, not guaranteed repeat purchase or bargaining power. Earlier retail exposure was concentrated in northern India; non-retail sales cannot be geographically separated from the source. [S01 pp.28–30,123–129,195]"

"The historical table retains original and restated scopes rather than manufacturing a smooth five-year story. FY26 operations EBIT is PBT + finance cost − other income = ₹29.2664 crore, and operating EBITDA is ₹35.6856 crore, 20.91% of revenue. Reported PAT is ₹15.1945 crore. Excluding after-tax other income gives an analyst normalization cross-check, not certified recurring earnings; lease equalization is not removed as a one-off merely because it is non-cash. Actual inventory markdowns, credit notes and confirmation adjustments are unresolved, so EARN remains NS. [S07]

FY26 cash-flow operating profit before working capital is ₹39.6967 crore. The line labeled 'Cash generated from/(used in) operations', negative ₹45.0514 crore, is actually the sum of working-capital movements. Adding it to pre-working-capital profit and subtracting ₹3.9311 crore tax yields the reported negative ₹9.2858 crore CFO. Treating the mislabeled subtotal as cash after working capital would invent a much worse CFO. The full line-by-line bridge and a ₹0.0002 crore aggregate rounding residual are retained. [S07 p.72]

Original FY24 reported CFO was positive ₹0.8859 crore but included ₹11.6650 crore short-term borrowing; stripped CFO is negative ₹10.7791 crore, matching the later comparative. Original FY25 CFO was negative ₹31.0320 crore; the FY26 comparative changes it to negative ₹22.8143 crore. The ₹8.2177 crore change reconciles exactly to ₹2.0074 crore deposit investment reclassification and ₹6.2103 crore current loan maturities entering other-current-liability operating movement. Removing the latter from latest FY25 CFO gives negative ₹29.0246 crore. FY26's ₹3.9141 crore increase in current maturities is similarly removed, giving negative ₹13.1999 crore. These adjustments identify financing classifications; they do not certify the remaining CFO as sustainable cash. [S04, S06, S07]

Across the latest FY24–FY26 comparable analytical rows, financing-stripped CFO/PAT is negative 177.28%. FY26 reported CFO/PAT is negative 61.11% and stripped CFO/PAT negative 86.87%. Negative cash is not caused by investing capex: the operating drain includes ₹55.6747 crore inventory growth, advances/deposits and other assets, partly offset by payables and other liabilities. After stripped CFO, ₹22.7671 crore capex and ₹9.7173 crore cash interest, the owner-cash diagnostic is negative ₹45.6843 crore. Reported investing movements in deposits/investments add another ₹10.3835 crore, although the ₹0.2809 crore difference from principal FD balance growth is accrued-interest classification, not proven new restricted principal. Gross debt grew ₹55.8734 crore and cash fell ₹0.1946 crore. [S07]

Gross debt is ₹96.8447 crore: ₹12.9214 crore long-term borrowing, ₹73.7989 crore short-term borrowing and ₹10.1244 crore current maturities disclosed separately in note 7. Excluding current maturities understates debt. Available cash is at most ₹0.5947 crore before any small escrow overlap; ₹12.11 crore lien-marked bank/NBFC deposits are not netted. Net debt is approximately ₹96.25 crore, 2.70 times operating EBITDA; EBIT/finance cost is 3.01 times. The BBB−/Stable rating is relevant contrary evidence, but the February rating disclosed bank utilization averaging 93% over the twelve months to December 2025 and July's ₹100 crore rated facilities include proposed amounts. Rated limits, a ₹120 crore borrowing authority and old ₹6.5 crore December cash are not verified October draw capacity. [S07, S14, S15, S17, S21–S22]

Receivables were ₹59.6271 crore net, versus ₹60.4921 crore prior year, with gross ₹60.5125 crore and ₹0.8854 crore provision. Average receivable days using total revenue as a credit-sales proxy are 128.47. Inventory rose from ₹17.4613 crore to ₹73.136 crore; compatible COGS is purchases plus inventory change, ₹68.7056 crore. Average inventory days are 240.65, while closing inventory/COGS is 388.54 days. The latter is a snapshot, not conventional average days. Average payable days on purchases are 30.36; compatible credit purchases are not separately disclosed, so the cash-cycle measure is a proxy. No ageing/markdown schedule for merchandise or independently verified post-period collections was located. Vendor advances of ₹28.8973 crore and other payable of ₹16.6210 crore need counterparty and settlement detail. [S07 notes 7,9,13,15,18]

Operating invested capital reconciles to financing invested capital exactly: ₹102.9897 crore in FY25 and ₹175.1059 crore in FY26. The bridge includes inventory, receivables, advances/government operating assets, operating liabilities, PPE, rent deposits and restricted collateral; it excludes cash, deferred tax, TDS and accrued non-operating interest, and adds back tax provisions on the financing side. Total committed capital includes illiquid collateral and deposits. The ₹72.1162 crore increase reconciles to net PPE investment ₹16.3479 crore, ONWC increase ₹37.2908 crore, rent deposits ₹8.3749 crore and restricted principal ₹10.1026 crore. At an assumed normalized 25.17% tax, average-capital ROIC is 15.75% and one-year incremental NOPAT/IC is 10.77%. These are accounting diagnostics, not mature-store project IRRs; no three/five-year CAP score is invented. [S07]

Operating leases remain rent expenses under AS. FY26 rent expense ₹17.8064 crore includes ₹2.7791 crore lease-equalization movement; subtracting it gives a ₹15.0273 crore cash-rent proxy, still subject to accrual timing. Future nominal commitments are ₹23.7661 crore next year, ₹100.0815 crore in years two to five and ₹76.9397 crore thereafter. The note also uses cancellable/12-month language, so contract enforceability and cancellation economics need clarification. No fabricated Ind AS lease liability is added to debt, and full nominal rent commitments are not capitalized while simultaneously deducting rent in valuation. The stress model retains cash rent and tests escalation. [S07 note 32]

October 8 issued 781,750 shares at ₹360 and 528,500 warrants at the same exercise price. Actual equity cash is ₹28.143 crore and warrant upfront cash ₹4.7565 crore. Issued capital is 10,391,550 shares; full warrants produce 10,920,050 shares and require another ₹14.2695 crore cash, conditional on exercise by April 2028. The authorized 720,735-option pool is not a verified outstanding grant; exercise price/proceeds are ND. A maximum pool-plus-warrant sensitivity gives 11,640,785 claims, not current issued capital. Historical weighted EPS is not today's current-share EPS. [S07, S09]"

"The monitoring register defines ten company-specific tests. These are research review points, not scheduled reminders or automatic trade instructions. The first priority is the next reviewed interim balance sheet and complete bank/current-maturity reconciliation, followed by signed resolution of recurring receivable/payable differences. Store productivity should be reported by opening cohort, ownership, age and closures, with inventory/deposits included in returns. Share issuance, warrant conversion and option grants need event-driven updates. A revenue beat without cash realization does not clear the hold; neither does a price fall.\n\nWarnings trigger investigation. Thesis breaks require evidence of unfinanceable obligations, a substantiated severe minority-protection failure, or repeated mature-cohort value destruction after relevant investment has seasoned. Temporary launch inventory and a slower opening quarter are not automatically thesis failures if cash is funded and mature cohorts remain sound."

"The most important failure variable is sale-through and cash recovery from incremental inventory and store capital. If immature stores need longer ramp-up, inventory must be discounted while rents and payroll continue. Lower gross margins weaken accrual earnings; slower wholesale collections and supplier advances raise cash needs; exhausted bank headroom or collateral requirements force equity at a discount. Existing holders can lose value even while total revenue grows. Security deposits and fit-outs are not reliable liquidation cash, and promoters' collateral guarantees do not become cash owned by minority shareholders. [S07, S12, S21]

The strongest contrary evidence to a purely bearish reading is the delivered 109-store network, provisional doubling of H1 sales, management's better older-store margin observations, an unmodified main/IFC audit opinion, no disclosed continuing borrowing default, an investment-grade rating and executed October financing. Those facts deserve weight. They do not establish audited cohort returns or explain all balance confirmations. Conversely, a modeled pre-entry shortfall is not proof the company actually defaulted: the necessary current bank data are missing.

Inventory and receivable write-down sensitivities quantify capital exposure with no assumed tax recovery. A 10% haircut to March inventory is ₹7.3136 crore; 10% of net receivables is ₹5.96271 crore. These are loss stresses, not evidence that a write-down is required. Any overlapping credit-note/provision adjustments must not be deducted twice. The linked bear also uses slower collections, longer stock holding, weaker margins, a bank-line contraction and release of legacy other payables, rather than valuing the same unsupported growth at a slightly lower multiple. The permanent-loss pathway is adverse recapitalization or irrecoverable stock/credit capital, not ordinary price volatility."

H1FY27 provisional revenue of ₹124 crore was announced on 1 October, against approximately ₹61 crore rounded in the announcement; using the prior reviewed ₹60.7276 crore gives 104.19% growth. The retail channel's change from 21% of FY25 sales to 40% of FY26 sales and 66 net additional stores explains why headline growth need not equal like-for-like consumer demand. Management's reported ₹4 lakh to ₹9 lakh monthly productivity for 42 stores mixes partial-year opening/ramp effects; it must not be relabeled 125% same-store growth. [S12–S13]

The source also records 22 Indian trademarks as of November 2024 and four design employees within a 190-person workforce in October 2024. Those are tangible organizational assets, not evidence of patent-like protection or current staffing. The prospectus expressly says manufacturing capacity utilization is inapplicable because the company is not a manufacturing concern. [S01 pp.133–134]"

"The source register gives primary URLs, dates, relevant pages and locally verified hashes where downloaded. Evidence V means a verified disclosed fact, not independently verified economic truth; C is calculation, M management attribution and A analyst assumption. Every model row is retained in the canonical record, including the full 60-session tape, historical vintages, monthly funding, annual summaries, reverse solutions, sensitivities and score bounds. Raw PDFs, OCR, screenshots, tax attachments, transfer helpers and credentials are excluded from reusable research archives.

Material gaps are current interim cash/debt and sanctioned undrawn headroom; complete quantified audit-difference resolution; MSME identification; receivable collections and credit notes after year end; inventory ageing/markdowns; exact mature/immature/company/franchise store cohorts and closures; comparable organic price/volume growth; counterparty detail for vendor advances, security-deposit liabilities and other payable; full original-to-restated revenue/PAT bridge; September/post-allotment ownership and encumbrances; lease cancellation commitments; actual option grants and exercise prices; and current litigation closure reconciliation. None is filled with zero or a peer average.

Forecast assumptions are nominal and deliberately separate from verified history. Retail/non-retail gross margins, mature sales, growth, cohort ramp, company-store mix, capex, rent inflation, working-capital days, liability release, bank-line reduction, tax, interest, rescue price/fees and terminal multiples are all sensitivity inputs. The most influential are inventory/collection intensity, mature-store profitability, opening liquidity and financing access. There is no claim to know contemporaneous market consensus; reverse expectations are analyst calculations from the observed price.

"The unchanged v 3.0 formulae are applied to thirteen canonical factors: GOV, MOAT, REV, DUR, CAP, CASH, BAL, EXEC, EARN and IAS factors R, D, P, L. REV, CAP and EARN remain NS because missing comparable organic growth, mature incremental-capital evidence and normalized earnings reliability are material. R, D and P are also NS: a mathematically linked scenario is not a defensible forecast when opening liquidity and unit economics are unverified. L is 7: the prescribed lower starting band is 9 for no more than two theoretical days, with two disclosed implementation deductions, one for lot granularity and one for observed one-price trading plus unverified depth/restrictions. This is not a hidden composite haircut. [E01–E20]\n\nCASH is 2 because negative financing-stripped cash conversion persists over three audited years, not merely because one year's capex is high. The default CASH≤3 growth-quality cap therefore applies to any computable GQS, but GQS remains NS, not 5. No governance or funding-failure numeric cap is applied: neither G1 nor G3 is an evidenced failure, and GOV is 4, not ≤3. Bounds use factor support from 1 through 10 without renormalizing known weights. IAS propagates incomplete BQS as an interval rather than substituting its midpoint. These are completeness bounds, not expected values or confidence intervals. All calculations use Decimal precision 34; only displays use half-up rounding. [Framework v 3.0; score audit]"
